work.title: Contra eos qui subintroductas habent virgines; Quod regulares feminae viris cohabitare non debeant

paragraphs.text: [?] By the same author: Against those who keep virgins as "spiritual companions" (subintroductae). 1. In the time of our forefathers there were two reasons that brought women to live under the same roof as men. One was marriage, which is ancient, just and reasonable, since God himself is its lawgiver: "For this reason," he says, "a man will leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh." The other was fornication, which is more recent than marriage, unjust and lawless, and was brought in by the wicked demons. But in our generation a third way has been devised as well. It is novel and strange, and anyone who wants to discover its cause is left at a loss. For there are some who take in girls who have never married and keep them settled at home permanently, without marriage or intercourse, shutting them in with themselves into extreme old age. They do not do it to have children, for they say they do not sleep with them. Nor do they do it out of licentiousness, for they say they keep them untouched. If anyone asks the reason, they have many reasons, well rehearsed, but none, in my opinion at least, that is reasonable or respectable. But let us not speak of these things yet, nor of their excuses for the moment. Instead let us bring into the open the reason we ourselves most suspect. What is it, then? Of course, if I miss the mark, any of you who wish may correct me. What, then, is the reason? It seems to me that living with women brings a certain pleasure, not only under the law of marriage but even without marriage and intercourse. Whether I am wrong I cannot say. For the moment I am giving you my own opinion, and perhaps not mine only but theirs as well. That they too think so is clear from this: they would not have scorned so much bad repute and so many scandals if the pleasure of this living together were not intense and tyrannical. If some are annoyed at our saying this, I will ask them to pardon us and not be indignant, for it is not willingly or lightly that I have chosen to take on this hostility. I am not so wretched and miserable as to want to offend everyone for no reason. But I am deeply pained and grieved when I see God's glory insulted, and the salvation of many slowly ebbing away because of this pleasure. Perhaps you are disturbed now to hear me say that this is pleasant, and that it stirs a keener desire than living together under the law of marriage, but once I have proved it you will agree yourselves. For in the case of a lawful wife, the [?] … [?] set before him a table laden with many most delightful

dishes, and forbade him with a severe threat to touch any of what lay before him. Would anyone choose to sit beside such a table and torment himself? I do not think so, for he would not reap as much pleasure from the sight as he would suffer dejection from the prohibition. And what if someone showed a pure, clear spring to a man burning with thirst, and allowed him not only not to drink from it but not even to touch it with his fingertips? Could any punishment be more bitter than this? 2. Here too I do not think anyone will object. So great is this evil that even those outsiders who are most skilled at examining such matters (I mean the nature of pleasure and pain) used no other method than this when they wanted to portray people being severely punished. They invented a myth and brought into it someone who had to pay the ultimate penalty. They set before him nothing else but a lavish feast, and showed him water flowing past, yet allowed him to enjoy none of it. As soon as he stretched out his hand, everything he saw flew away, and this went on forever. That was the manner of punishment in the pagan myth. And one of the philosophers, seeing one of his companions kiss a handsome youth, was astonished and said that a man who dared to kindle such a furnace within himself by a kiss would just as easily leap headlong into fire. For my part, I would not say that these men kiss or fondle the women who live with them. But if some accuse them of this, I will try to show that if they go that far they bring on themselves a torment more bitter still than the first. For if sight alone causes so much pain, then when touch is added, an enjoyment much grosser than sight, it raises a greater flame, produces sharper anguish, and makes the beast more savage. The more we feed desire and the stronger the nourishment we give it, the more our pain is intensified. A man sitting beside the table and the spring is not so pained by looking as when he is permitted to touch with his hand and then prevented from tasting. In the same way, those permitted to touch virgin bodies are punished more severely by touch than by sight, and bring on themselves a more bitter pain from their frustration. But why do we need to reason about these things from outside sources? The verdict of God, which carries more weight than all of these, shows that this is so. When he wished to punish Adam, he did not settle him far from paradise but right beside it, so that the sight of the place he longed for would be a perpetual punishment: he saw it constantly but was not permitted to enjoy it. But perhaps someone might say: "If this is so bitter by nature, how is it that most people pursue it so eagerly?" To this I would reply that this very fact is the greatest proof of their extreme sickness. For this is the habit of the sick: to reap some cold, brief pleasure and so prepare a long punishment for themselves. You can see this in people with a fever, who are unwilling to hold out for a little while, and for the sake of some brief gratification [?] …

[?] … than is fitting. When he was discussing the nature of foods, showing that they were clean and freeing his disciples from the Jewish observance, Peter came in and said, "They were scandalized." "Let them be," he said. Not only did he disregard them, he even accused them, saying, "Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted." In this way he annulled the law about foods. But when the collectors of the two-drachma tax came to Peter and said, "Does your teacher not pay the two drachmas?", he did not do as he had done before. Instead he took care to avoid scandal and said: "But so that we do not scandalize them, go to the sea and cast a hook. Take the first fish that comes up, and you will find a stater in its mouth. Take it and give it to them for me and for you." Do you see him both taking care and not taking care? Here there was no urgent need for the glory of the Only-begotten to be revealed. How could there be, when he was taking pains to keep it hidden and ordered many people not to say that he was the Christ? That is why no harm came from paying the two drachmas, but great evils would have arisen from not paying them: people would have turned away from him as from a tyrant and a rebel, an enemy of the whole city who was plunging them into the utmost danger. For the same reason, when they wanted to seize him and make him king, he fled far away, rejecting this suspicion by a wide margin. In the other case, however, what was being accomplished was necessary. So it was useful and timely for him to disregard the scandal, for the sake of a greater achievement. For the time had now come not to hold back, out of consideration for the Jews, those who were about to ascend to the highest philosophy. It was time to release them, since the moment was calling them to purity of soul, and not to keep them in bodily observance but to let them be freed from that lowliness. So too Paul, following his teacher, both disregards those who are scandalized and does not disregard them. He says: "I please everyone in everything, not seeking my own advantage but that of the many, so that they may be saved." If Paul overlooks his own advantage to secure that of others, what punishment would we not deserve? We cannot bear even to give up what harms us in order to secure the advantage of others. Instead we gladly destroy others along with ourselves, when we could save both ourselves and them. That is why, when Paul sees that the gain is great, greater than the harm of the scandal, he disregards those who are scandalized. But when there is no gain and the only result would be scandal, he chooses to do and suffer anything to prevent it. And he does not reason as we do, or say, "Why are they weak? Why are they so unreasonably affected by this?" On the contrary, he spares them most of all precisely because they are unreasonably affected, because they are weak. 4. Tell me, what reasonable excuse can a man give for being scandalized by someone who eats meat and drinks wine? God laid down this law from the beginning. Yet even so, if anyone is scandalized by these things, Paul abstains from them. "I will not eat meat," he says, "or drink wine, so that I may not scandalize my brother." And he did not say what we say: "Am I to be held accountable for the irrationality of others?" or "If someone happens to take offense for no reason, do I deserve to be punished?" [?]

[?] … soared above all the devil's nets. He was the first and the only one to show such endurance, surpassing all iron and adamant in the self-control of his soul and cutting down the devil's strength. Yet he so feared this kind of wrestling, and thought it so impossible for a man living with a virgin to remain unharmed and pure, that he kept far away not only from such living together but even from a glance that happens simply by chance. He made a law for his eyes not even to look at a virgin at all. For he knew clearly, he knew, that not only the man who lives with a virgin but even the man who looks curiously at a virgin's face will find it difficult, perhaps impossible, to escape the harm that comes from it. That is why he said: "And I will not gaze at a virgin." 5. Perhaps Job seems to you too small to compete with, though we are not worthy even of his dunghill. Still, if you think his example falls short of your own greatness of soul, consider Paul, the loudest-voiced herald of the truth. He traveled the whole world and could speak those words so full of wisdom: that it was no longer he who lived but Christ in him, that he had been crucified to the world and the world to him, and that he died daily. Yet after such great grace of the Spirit, after such displays of struggle, after unspeakable dangers, after so exact a philosophy, he showed us and made plain that as long as we breathe and wear this flesh we need struggles and toil. Chastity can never be achieved without effort; this trophy needs much sweat and labor. So he spoke thus: "I pummel my body and enslave it, so that after preaching to others I myself may not be disqualified." He said this to show the revolt of the flesh, the frenzy of desire, the constant war, and the life of struggle he led. That is why Christ too, showing how difficult the matter is, did not allow anyone even to look casually at women's faces, and threatened to punish those who look in that way with the punishment of adulterers. And when Peter said that it is not expedient to marry, Christ did not make a law against marrying. Instead, pointing out how weighty the matter is, he said: "Let anyone who can accept this accept it." We hear too that in our own generation many men bind their whole bodies with iron, clothe themselves in sackcloth, and climb to the mountaintops. They live in constant fasting, all-night vigils and sleeplessness, show every kind of hardship, and forbid all women to set foot in their room or hut. Even training themselves in this way, they barely overcome the madness of desire. But you say that even if I see a man living with a virgin, attached to her, living in luxury, ready to give up his own soul sooner than his companion, choosing to suffer and do anything rather than be parted from the woman he longs for, I should not suspect anything wicked or think that desire is at work, but

But it is not toward those who have bodies, my good sir, but toward those who live with stones that one should take that attitude. You perhaps do not believe it because of your great chastity, but I have heard people tell [?] …

[?] … You were commanded to carry the cross and follow Christ, but you have thrown the cross away, as soft soldiers throw away their shields, and now you sit beside the spindle and the wool-basket. By another, more shameful method you have opened the door back into the present life. For it is not so shameful for married men to manage these things as it is for you, who pretend to have leapt away from the things of this life, to slip back into them under another guise. That is why we get a reputation everywhere as gluttons, parasites, flatterers and slaves of women: we have thrown to the ground all the nobility given us from above and traded it for earthly servility and cheapness. Those noble men of that time did not choose to distribute money to the widows, even when there was so much complaint because no one was managing it. They considered this beneath their philosophy and entrusted it to others. But we are not ashamed to increase other people's wealth to the ruin of its owners. We are in no better state than the eunuchs who busy themselves with such things, who are ordered every day to carry their blood and their lives in their hands instead of great weapons. "What then? Must we stand by while all the virgin's property is seized, carried off and plundered by relatives, by servants, by strangers, or even by her own household?" A fine reward indeed we will give the virgin for not marrying, for not loving the present world but choosing Christ above everything, if we leave her exposed to anyone who wants to rob her of her possessions! But how much better it would have been for her to marry and use her husband to manage these affairs than to remain unmarried and yet trample on her covenant with God, outrage so holy and awesome a thing, and drag others too into the shipwreck of her own evils! How can you say she chose Christ above everything, when Christ cries out, "You cannot serve God and mammon"? How has she hated the world and the things of this life, when you persuade her to be excited by the desires of the world? Which married woman will you ever be able to advise to disregard money, while you are helping the virgin build up her wealth? And when will you let this very virgin be devoted to the Lord and undistracted, when you spend your whole life and zeal on her affairs? When will the virgin be able to live as a philosopher, when she sees you, a man, thinking it terrible that her money might be scattered? How will she bear to disregard her losses, when she sees you doing and suffering everything to increase her present wealth? God does not want us to be freed from affairs in this way, but by despising possessions and renouncing all worldly things. But you do not allow it, and you do not let God's law prevail. "What then," someone says, "if she needs the protection of others, and suffers many indignities?" And are these things not unworthy of a virgin now? Nothing is so unworthy of a virgin as being rich and surrounded by a mass of business. And what if she orders other things besides, such as lending gold at interest, and calls us to handle the transactions, and we refuse, and so she brings in others? Will we be to blame? And what if she sets up other petty trades, illiberal and unseemly, and then, when we will not cooperate, needs others [?] …

[?] … effort you need to gather them, so readily do they lie before everyone who is willing to stretch out a hand. If you have money, spend it on these women. If you are strong, bring your bodily service here. Here too you will see many tasks that need bodily service, expense of money and running about. It is hard work to find lodgings for them, to prepare medicines, to buy beds, clothes and suitable food, and to see to everything else, even if there were only ten women suffering from such diseases. But as it is, our city is full of them; you will find a thousand and twice as many. These are the ones who need protection, these are the abandoned, these are the ones lying on the ground. This is almsgiving, this is love of humanity. This rises to the glory of God and brings benefit to those who act, to those who suffer, and to those who look on. For it would be more just to help the weaker rather than the strong, the old rather than the young, and those who lack even the food they need rather than those of moderate means. It would be more just to help women loathed by most people because their afflictions are so hard to bear, rather than women desired by many, and women who can both avert any disgrace already incurred and add good repute, rather than those who bring disgrace upon you. Show, then, that you do these things for God by caring for these women. But if you will not even dream of seeing them, and instead go around hunting the good-looking and the young, your real motive for this illiberal hunt is intolerable, and you put forward another that seems respectable: protection. You may deceive people, but you will not deceive the incorruptible tribunal while you act for one reason and allege another. For you say that you do everything for God, but what you do is the work of God's enemies. Causing his name to be blasphemed and slandered is the work of God's enemies. [?] But I will make another supposition as well. Let us suppose that the man who says this is telling the truth, that he is pure of all desire, and that he takes on this protection out of nothing but piety. Even so we shall not find him free from punishment. If he had no other occasions to show his piety, he should have done it without souls being scandalized. Really, even then he should not have engaged in such things, where the loss is greater than the gain. For tell me, how can the two be equal: protecting one or two virgins for the sake of bodily affairs, and scandalizing countless multitudes in their souls? Still, the charge would not be so grave in that case. But when you find countless ways that are free from accusation and scandal and offer greater gain, why do you entangle yourself in trouble rashly and in vain, undermine your own profit, and build precariously and shamefully, when you could build safely and with great honor? Do you not know that a Christian's life must shine brilliantly everywhere? And that anyone who has disgraced his reputation will be useless everywhere from then on, and will gain nothing great even if he happens to achieve great things? "For if the salt has lost its taste," he says, "what will it be salted with?" God wants us to be salt and light and leaven, so that others too can share in the benefit we bring. For if people living blameless lives could barely turn back the negligent, then if we also give them a handle [?] …

and you make it worse every day. Who, then, will excuse you? Who will pardon you? No one at all. God and the saints take great care that his name should not be blasphemed. This is not because God needs glory from us, for he lacks nothing and is perfect, but because the thing does people great harm. When the name and glory of God have been slandered in their eyes, it no longer does them any good; and if God, once slandered, does no one any good, much less do we. 9. Let us therefore do everything we can so that no occasion of offense arises. Even if they accuse us unjustly, let us persuade them and clear away the charges. Let us imitate the saints, who were so zealous for God's glory that they despised even their own for the sake of his. Let us not throw everything away and trample on it, and then think it defense enough to say that we bought the virgin a cloak and shoes and arranged everything else well for her bodily comfort. "And who," he says, "will manage our household affairs? Who will look after our belongings? Who will be in charge while we are out, if there is no woman in the house?" For they say this too, though it contradicts what they said before and is more shameful still. None of it troubles them, and they feel no shame [241], like drunkards who blurt out whatever comes into their heads. So let us not grow weary either, even if what they say is such that it deserves no answer. Let us not grow weary of answering them and reasoning gently with them until we free them from this drunkenness, as far as it lies with us. I am ashamed, and I blush, to set about refuting things that they do not blush to put forward. Still, the shame must be borne for the good of those who feel none. It would be absurd for us to accuse them of disregarding the brothers who are scandalized, and then neglect their own cure out of shame. Tell me, what are these domestic affairs that they think need the virgin's help to manage? Are there crowds of maidservants, barbarians and newly bought, who have to be kept in order for wool-working and other service? Are there storerooms full of money and costly garments, so that a guard must sit inside at all times, and the virgin's eyes must be set up like a wall against the servants' thieving? Are dinners and drinking parties held constantly, so that the house must be kept elegant and the cooks and table-servants must enjoy the virgin's supervision? Are there many kinds of constant expenses, so that someone must always be in charge, to keep some things carefully and to stop others from draining out of the house to no purpose? "None of these," he says. "She is there to look after my little chest and my cloak and the rest of my poverty, to set my table, make my bed, light the fire, wash my feet, and provide every other comfort." Then for this small and paltry comfort are we to bring on ourselves so heavy an accusation and endure so many reproaches? How much better and more easily a brother would do these services! A man is by nature stronger than a woman, more suited to our needs, and not so expensive. A woman, being more delicate, needs a softer bed and finer clothes, and perhaps a girl to wait on her in turn, and she does not give us as much service as she herself requires. [Note:] Savile reads σοι χρεία βαρβάρων ("you need barbarians"). Below, the same editor reads ἀλλὰ ταμείων καὶ χρημάτων πολλῶν ("but of storerooms and much money").

insulted in such ways, and having this as his only consolation for his own troubles, against the one who has grieved him. The man who lives with a poor woman will not deal with silversmiths, since poverty does not allow it, nor will he wait on perfume-sellers. But he will often pester shoemakers, weavers, embroiderers and dyers. Why should I list all the indecency: how they go into workshops selling warp and woof, how they go round the marketplace hunting for these same things again? That is what happens in the houses; in the marketplaces they put up with things far more ridiculous than these. 10. As for the church, the shame cannot even be described [245]. As though no place should be left unaware of their disgrace and this servile slavery, they display all their lack of self-control even in this holy and most awe-inspiring place. What is worse, they even pride themselves on what they ought to be ashamed of. They meet the women outside at the doors, act as their eunuchs and clear a way for them, and they lead the way with their heads held high while everyone watches. They do not shrink with shame; they even exult. At the very time of the most awe-inspiring mysteries they perform many services to please the women, and give many onlookers a handle against them. And the wretched, miserable women, who ought to stop them from such attentions, preen themselves and are proud of it. Yet if anyone meant to call down a curse on these women or on those men, what harsher curse could he find than this: to have countless witnesses of their licentiousness and to disgrace themselves before the eyes of all? Why should I tell how much is thrown into disorder in the churches themselves for these women's sake, and how many of God's affairs many people neglect so as not to provoke them? Why do I say "provoke"? If someone merely gives them a sullen or unfriendly look, the men will choose to endure anything rather than let her suffer that. But how long are we going to disgrace ourselves by recounting all their doings? That was not our purpose, since we would need many long speeches to go through everything. Or rather, it is impossible to tell everything even if we wanted to; even putting together a few things out of many would be enough to make a long speech. But that is not why we came. We mentioned even these things unwillingly, to sting a little those of our hearers who have sense. What remains is to exhort and entreat. I beg and implore you, I throw myself at your knees, I make every supplication: be persuaded. Let us recover from this drunkenness and come to ourselves. Let us recognize the honor God has given us and listen to Paul crying out, "Do not become slaves of human beings." Let us stop being slaves to women, to the common ruin of us all. Christ wants us to be noble soldiers and athletes. He did not arm us with spiritual weapons so that we would take on the service of worthless girls, busy ourselves with wool and looms and such services, sit beside women as they spin and weave, and spend every day stamping women's ways and words onto our own souls. He armed us to strike the invisible powers ranged against us, to smite the devil who commands them, to drive off the savage battle lines of the demons, to tear down their strongholds, to [Note:] Savile reads δεῖται ("needs"); Morel reads δεῖ ("must").

these women stray from the road proper to them because of those men, and give them this wicked and ruinous return [246]. They adorn themselves too elaborately, take great pains over a languid posture and gait, and chatter about unseemly things all day long. Since they see the men delighting in these licentious manners and words, they practice everything by which they can hold them captive. But if we are willing to recover a little and come to ourselves, we shall win both them and ourselves and everyone else. Just as we are now accountable for the ruin of many, so then we shall receive the reward for the salvation of all, and what we now enjoy in shame we shall then enjoy with great honor. Tell me, do you want to be honored by women? It is above all unworthy of a spiritual man to crave honor of that kind. Even so, this too will come then, when we stop seeking it. It is human nature to despise those who fawn on us and to admire those who do not flatter, and women's nature tends to feel this more strongly. A woman becomes unbearable when she is flattered, and above all she admires those who will not give way and bow to her untimely desires. You yourselves will bear me witness to this. As things are, not only outsiders but the very women who live with you laugh at you, if not openly then in their hearts, and they pride themselves on this harsh tyranny. Then, however, they will all admire you and be amazed at your freedom. If you do not believe our words, ask the women themselves whom they praise and value more: those who are their slaves or those who govern them; those who submit and do and endure everything to please them, or those who put up with none of it and are ashamed of their wicked commands. If they are willing to tell the truth, they will certainly name the latter. Or rather, no answer is needed, since the facts cry it out. "But," someone says, "the man who lives with her gains in pleasure, feasting his eyes on the sight of virgins." Even if this were so, that is exactly why it ought to be avoided. But it has now been sufficiently shown to you that such a thing is not pleasant, and that the opposite is: not enjoying this sight. Add to this, I ask you, the gladness that comes from conscience. Nothing usually gladdens us so much as a good conscience and good hopes. Or do you seek this for the sake of comfort? It has been shown that this too is easier when a brother lives with you. As it is, you are no different from a slave; seeking comfort, you have found the harshest slavery. Then, however, you will stand clear of this service and be among those who give orders, not those who take them. On the one side there is grief instead of pleasure, shame instead of glory, slavery instead of freedom, toil instead of rest, and on top of this the blasphemy of God, so great a ruin, scandals, unending punishment and the loss of countless good things. On the other side there is everything opposite: glory, honor, pleasure, boldness, freedom, the salvation of souls, the inheritance of the kingdom, release from punishment. Why, then, shall we not exchange the one for the other? I do not know, unless someone simply wishes to destroy himself. For we shall have no defense left, and no pardon. Even if none of these things were so, one ought to endure everything for the sake of [Note:] Savile reads αἰδοῦς ("modesty"); Morel reads ὁδοῦ ("road"). Savile reads μετὰ τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ χάριν ("after the grace of God").

cutting himself a road of amusement and delight. But when he had recovered a little from it, and had been able to look up, as if from some dark abyss, to the light of philosophy, he uttered that lofty saying, worthy of heaven: "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity." You too, if you are willing, will pass this verdict on this untimely pleasure, and a loftier one, if you withdraw yourselves a little from this evil habit. And yet Solomon, living in earlier times, was not required to reach any great exactness in philosophy. The old law did not forbid luxury, nor did it call the enjoyment of other pleasures superfluous and vain. Even so, he was able to see how unprofitable they are and to condemn their great vanity. We, however, are called to a higher way of life, we are climbing a loftier summit, and we have stripped for greater contests. What else are we commanded to do but to live like those spiritual and bodiless powers above? How, then, is it not shameful and deserving of severe punishment to be seen as far inferior to him? We not only fail to rise above what is permitted, as he did, but we even lay hands on what is forbidden and carries unbearable punishment. Consider what it means to nourish a wicked love in the soul; to look at a woman with desire; to gaze closely at beauty that belongs to another; to disgrace oneself and harm the weaker; to give many handles to the Greeks and many to the Jews; to trip up both our own people and outsiders; to produce much blasphemy against the glory of God; to take on the duties of a slave; to thrust oneself into the turmoil of worldly affairs; to toss away to the devil the freedom given to us and take the harshest tyranny in exchange; to be a laughingstock to friends and a reproach to enemies; to bring an evil reputation on the whole Church; to disgrace the venerable dignity of virginity; to give many pretexts to those who want to live wantonly; and to bring about many other evils besides, for it is impossible to perceive or put into words everything they suffer through these practices. All of this belongs among the things strictly forbidden, which carry unbearable punishment. So even if there is some small pleasure in it, setting all these things against it [?] ages of ages. Amen.

THAT WOMEN UNDER RULE SHOULD NOT LIVE WITH MEN. 1. Alas, my soul! With the prophet it is fitting for me too to say this now, once, twice and many times: Alas, my soul! What a great thing, how full of philosophy! Virginity has been outraged. The veil that separated it from marriage has been taken away, torn down by shameless hands. The holy of holies has been trampled. Things venerable and full of awe have become profane and open to all. What was more venerable than marriage has been dragged down and brought so low that married women are now counted more blessed. When virginity was ranked with marriage, it always held first place [249] and complete precedence. Now it has not been able to keep even the second rank, but somewhere far off, toward the last [Note:] Tilmann [?], cited by Savile: [?] τὰς ἐχούσας ἄνδρας συνεισ[?] ("those who have husbands" [?]). Savile reads καὶ τὸ δέ. Savile reads μὲν γὰρ ἕνεκεν. Below, the same editor reads Ἕλληνας.

[?] so much rage he breathed out against this flock, since he saw that it was above all this battalion that made Christ's army brilliant. He has tried to disgrace it so thoroughly that it would now be better if those who attempt to pursue the life in this way were not virgins at all. The cause of all the evils is that the thing has stopped at the name, and the whole of it has been confined to the mouth, which is the smallest part of virginity. The more essential things, which above all show what virginity is, are neglected. They take no account of modest dress, of the quietness that befits virgins, of compunction, or of anything else of that kind. They speak freely about everything, laugh at the wrong moments, and are more languid and affected than the loose women of the brothel, setting traps on every side for those who look at them. They push themselves into the indecency of prostitutes, as if competing with them and striving to carry off first prize for shame. Tell me, how can we any longer exclude such a virgin from the ranks and company of those women, when she does the same things they do, deceiving the hearts of young men; when she is flighty and dissolute; when she grinds the same drugs, mixes the same cups and prepares the same hemlock? "But she does not say, 'Come, let us roll in love,' nor, 'I have sprinkled my bed with saffron and my couch with cinnamon.'" Would that it were your bed and couch, and not your clothes and your body! Those women hide the bait at home, but you carry the snare around everywhere, and spreading out the wings of pleasure you parade it through the marketplace. "But you did not converse with anyone, nor did you speak those harlot's words, 'Come, let us roll in love.'" You did not say it with your tongue, but you said it with your bearing. You did not utter it with your mouth, but you uttered it with your walk. You did not call out with your voice, but you called through your eyes more clearly than any voice. "But having called, you did not give yourself." Even so you are not free of sin. This too is another kind of fornication. You have remained pure of the outrage, but of the bodily one, not the one of the soul. The whole sin has been completed by you, if not through intercourse, then through the eyes. Tell me, why do you call out to the passers-by? Why do you kindle the fire? How can you think yourself pure of sin when you have committed all of it [250]? You have made a complete adulterer of the man who has been caught by this bearing of yours. How then can you not be an adulteress, when your work stands convicted of adultery? His madness is your doing. Everyone knows that a woman who makes adulterers could never escape the punishment for adultery. You sharpened the sword, you armed the hand, you drove the armed hand against the wretched soul. How then can you escape punishment for this murder? Tell me, whom do we hate and turn away from? Whom do lawgivers and judges punish? Those who drink the deadly drugs, or those who mix the cup, prepare the poison and destroy people by their art? Do we not pity those who drink, as people who have been wronged, and condemn the others by every vote? It is no defense for them to say, "I did not harm myself; I destroyed someone else." For this very reason they pay a heavier penalty. And you, wretched and miserable woman, having mixed this deadly cup, [Note:] Savile reads καὶ ἐν τῷ σώματι ("and in the body"); Morel, however, reads καὶ ἐν τῷ στόματι ("and in the mouth"). Savile reads πάντοθεν μηχανώμεναι τοῖς ὁρῶσιν ἐγγίσαι ("contriving on every side to get near those who look at them"); Morel reads πάντοθεν μηχανήματα τοῖς ὁρῶσιν ἐνιεῖσαι ("setting traps on every side for those who look at them"). Shortly after, Savile reads πεπορνευμένων [?]; and νέων ἐξάπτεσθαι καρδίας ("to inflame the hearts of young men"), wrongly. Savile reads εἶπας both times. ἀναπνεῖν ὅλως ("to breathe at all") [?]. ἀλλά.

Bethsaida, he no longer used counsels or signs, only lamentation, repeatedly pronouncing "Woe" over the cities, as we do over the dying. Blessed Paul too, imitating his teacher, never stopped lamenting, all his life long, those who had fallen, who stayed down where they fell and would not get up [?]. He lamented them so bitterly that he wrote this very thing to the Romans with a strong affirmation: "I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites." Do you see how forceful the words are, how much anguish of heart they reveal? He mourns those of the faithful who limp and are tossed about as though he himself were caught in those evils. "Who is weak," he says, "and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?" He did not say, "I grieve," but, "I burn," wanting to show through the image of burning how unbearable and incurable the pain is. Let us, then, imitate both our Master and our fellow servant. No small reward [252] will be laid up for us for these laments and dirges, just as no ordinary blame from God awaits those who pass by the sufferings of their own members without sympathy. One can see the first from that most steadfast man Ezekiel, and the second from blessed Micah. Ezekiel says that when the Jews had reached the extreme of wickedness and deserted to the wickedness of idols, God commanded that a mark be placed on the foreheads of those who groaned and grieved over what was happening. (One ought not merely to groan, but to grieve deeply [?].) Those people said and did nothing to correct what was happening. Yet because they contributed only what was in their power [?], the loving God honored them so highly that they were counted worthy of great safety. Micah, along with his other charges of gluttony, drunkenness and anointing with perfumes, also brought this charge of lacking sympathy, saying, "[?] they felt no pain at the affliction of Joseph." Again he reproached those who live in Aenan, saying, "She did not come out to mourn [?] for the house next to her." If God is angry [?], and the one who suffers with those being punished [?], what pardon will he deserve who does not grieve with those who fall into wickedness? Even [?] when God punishes, we ought to grieve with those who are punished, for not even God himself wishes to do this when he punishes: "For he does not desire the death of the sinner," he says. If, then, the one who punishes does not wish to punish, much more ought we to grieve with those who are punished. Perhaps in this way we shall call them out; perhaps we shall win them back. For even if they have perished, let us still offer them what care remains, and let us lament [?] [Note:] [?] συμβουλαῖς ("counsels"). [?] κατοδύρεσθαι ("to lament"). [?] Savile reads ἀνάπτετε ("you kindle"); Morel reads ἀνάπτεται ("is kindled").

[?]… But let us grant for now that she has risen above all these nets, that she is pure in every respect, free from all harm, and remains a virgin. What does this have to do with what we have said? For this is the most terrible thing of all, and full of countless tears: she endured so much toil guarding her body carefully on every side, and then emptied out all that toil and poured away all that labor by blaspheming Christ. She spared the glory of her flesh but did not spare God's glory. She did everything to keep her body untouched, but she gave no thought at all to keeping his glory from being insulted and put to shame before the many. Would that she were not doing and contriving everything by which God's glory is slandered! “And how am I doing this?” she asks. By shutting men up in the house with you and having them sit beside you all the time. If you want to have men living with you, you should not have chosen virginity; you should have married. It is far better to marry in that way than to be a virgin in this way. Neither does God condemn such a marriage, nor do people slander it, for it is an honorable thing that wrongs no one and harms no one. But this virginity in the company of men is slandered by everyone more harshly than fornication. It has lost its proper rank and rolled down to somewhere near the very pit of fornication. No one would bear to count among the virgins a woman who does not care for the things of the Lord but takes on countless adulterers, nor would anyone count her among the married. The married woman cares how she may please one husband. You please countless men, and men who are not joined to you by the law of marriage but in some other way that everyone slanders and condemns. So I fear that, driven out of both places, you will turn out to be ranked with dishonored women. Even from the very name they are given, if anyone wished to judge these matters, we will once again have nothing to say in reply. When the couple go out into the marketplace, or when there is talk about them at home, those who discuss this strange pairing and want to say whose woman she is do not call her his mother, for she did not give birth to him. Nor do they call her his sister, for she was not born of the same birth pangs. Nor do they call her his wife, for she has not lived with him under the law of marriage. Nor do they use any other name of kinship that is permitted and established by law. They use the shameful and ridiculous name. I could not bear to say it myself, so much do I hate and turn away from the very term, and the name for this cohabitation sickens me. “But you have not given birth, nor been in labor.” What could be more shameful than this defense? What could be more wretched, when a virgin wants to appear a virgin on the very grounds where many women who prostitute themselves can also take refuge? “But those women are proved to be debauched by other evidence,” she says. What other evidence, tell me? Their dress, their glance, their walk, the lovers they catch. You have described the character of a harlot well for us. But take care that these signs and proofs do not convict you before they convict her, for you too procure many such lovers for yourself, and with the same nets. And if you do not stand at the brothel door calling to passers-by, you keep men shut up inside all the time, which is far worse, and for no other reason than so that [Textual notes: for “is slandered,” Savile reads “was slandered”; punctuate thus: “all the time, which is far worse”.]

for there is no other way for you to be freed from this disgrace. These things you have said belong less to you than to those who grieve over your disgrace. Even if the man's service were ten thousand times more useful, you still should not accept it at the cost of so much reproach. When God's glory is insulted, let no excuse seem so pressing as to persuade us to overlook so great an evil. Even if we had to die ten thousand times a day to keep this from happening, we ought to endure it with great joy. How much less should we let so great an evil pass for the sake of comfort and worldly need! Listen to how Paul fears and trembles at this, and how far beyond what was required: “It would be better for me to die,” he says, “than that anyone should make my boast empty.” He chose to die so that his boast might not be emptied. Will we, in order to remove stumbling blocks, not even give up a little ease? How will we ever be saved? Yet being deprived of praise is not the same as falling under accusation, or anywhere near it. Even if that had happened to Paul, he would not have offended God, for God himself had commanded him to live by the gospel. Nevertheless he chose to die rather than give up what he had achieved. And we, who throw God's commands into confusion everywhere, and know that we will pay the heaviest penalty for it, cannot bring ourselves to disregard an ill-timed and frigid habit? What pardon will there be for us? As I said before, even if most of your needs could only be met by a man, when so much disgrace arose from the arrangement you ought to choose to die rather than allow it. But when everything can be done more easily, and very simply, by a woman, what pardon will there be for you who pamper yourselves like this and treat your own salvation with contempt? Tell me, when he provides these things for you, will you not provide him with some service in return? That is obvious to everyone. How much better neither to give such things in return nor to receive them. Better to spend on your own needs the time and labor you spend on his comfort than to toil at heavier tasks and disgrace your reputation besides. “But I provide him no service.” Then he must do everything for himself: make the bed, cook, light the fire, and do all the other such tasks. Not even a slave would put up with serving if he got nothing from his master. “But he puts up with everything,” she says, “out of the fear of God and for the reward stored up for this service. He will be grateful to be given orders, even though he gets nothing from us.” How then will we stop the mouths of the shameless? If you bear witness to such piety in him, if he so trembles and fears God's commands that he thinks himself cheaper than any slave and endures everything while getting nothing from you, then before all this he ought to have cared for God's glory and good name. As it is, one and the same soul cannot, at one and the same time, show such obedience and such contempt toward God's commands, trembling at them one moment and the next taking no account of the insult to the very one who gave the laws. For to be pure of pleasure and to feel nothing human at all…

[?]… let us press harder, for in contending for such things you sin against Christ himself. Do you not hear Moses saying again and again in the Old Testament, “God is a jealous God”? And God himself saying, “I have been jealous for Jerusalem”? And Paul crying out in the New, “For I am jealous over you with a godly jealousy”? This alone, if nothing else, would be enough to turn back a soul that is not gravely sick and numbed. Fearful as it is, it is sweeter than it is fearful. There could never be jealousy unless warm and fervent love were already there beneath it. So this is proof of God's vehement and fiery love and friendship. Jealousy in God is not a passion. He often uses this word because he wants to express his unspeakable tenderness. Yet we, utterly insensible, fall into human attachments. We insult the one who loves us so vehemently and court in every way those who can do us no good. What good can this frigid cohabitation do you, wretched woman, to match the treasures it casts you out of? Consider: it brings you down from heaven, drives you from the spiritual bridal chamber, separates you from the heavenly Bridegroom, and procures for you deathless punishment and torments without end. In exchange for these, if the man who lives with you supplied ten thousand gold mines, if he were more subject to you than slaves bought with silver, if he set you in greater honor and comfort than the empress herself, ought you not still to hate him and turn away from him as a destroyer and an enemy, as one who takes away more than he gives? The matter before you concerns the good things in heaven, the kingdom there, immortal life, glory beyond words. And you talk about earthly things and court like a master the man who seems useful in them. Do you not sink with shame, or pray for the earth to open up for you so that you may depart from here? But you plead the weakness of female nature, the management of human needs, comfort at home, inventing and putting together excuses that do not exist. Even so, you will not escape the notice of people with sense. There is not, there is not, any comfort that forces you into such indecency. A woman, if she wishes, will be enough to serve not only herself but many others. From the beginning, when the man was given the affairs of public life, she was allotted the keeping of the house and the management of everything indoors. So it is not because you need comfort that you draw men inside. “Then why?” someone says. “For fornication and licentiousness?” I would not say that, God forbid. Indeed, I never stop rebuking those who say it, and I wish I could persuade them. “What then is the reason that makes the thing so desirable to us?” she asks. Love of vainglory. Just as for the men a frigid and wretched pleasure brings about this sharing of a dwelling, so for these women it is desire for honor. The whole human race is vainglorious, so to speak, but the female sex especially so. When they do not need comfort, as has been shown, and are not being corrupted with these men, it is plain that this is the only thing left to suspect. 6. Since we have found the very root of the evil, come, let us leave off accusing and instead exhort and persuade them that, just as the men who live with them seem to enjoy pleasure but surround themselves with greater torment (for that… [?] women will be astonished, and men will all admire you

together, as a virgin who attends on the Bridegroom without distraction. Then not only your own people but Greeks and Jews too, and the whole human race, will welcome you. So if you are eager for glory, travel this road, not the opposite one. Then they will no longer call you so-and-so's woman, but Christ's, and no one could ever give you any other adornment equal to this. Tell me, are these small things, sung and spread around every day in the marketplace, in houses, and in other cities: “So-and-so, a young girl, very young and very beautiful, who could have attracted many protectors if she had wished, did not wish it. She chose to endure and suffer anything at all rather than betray the friendship of Christ and destroy the flower of her chastity. Blessed is she, twice and three times and many times over! What good things she will enjoy, what a crown she will receive, what a reward she will reap, vying with the bodiless powers themselves!” These and similar things everyone will say about her, and they will hold her up to their daughters as a model to imitate. If anyone wants to encourage a girl who is living decently, or to bring one who has been corrupted to her senses, everyone will again bring her praises forward. And not only then: whenever there is any talk about virginity at all, everyone will praise her, not only those who live decently but also those who tried hard and did everything to win her, and were then scorned and disdained. She will enjoy this much glory, and much more than I have described. But the woman who has men living with her will meet with the very opposite. First, when some foul people attack virginity, both women will come to mind in such gatherings, but the one opens the mouths of the defenders and the other the mouths of the accusers. Then, when someone needs to be corrected and set right, the one is brought forward like an astringent medicine that can check rot, and she adorns the teacher's mouth. The other stands with the disgraced woman, even if she is not present, punished and put to shame. Each time a woman goes astray, she too must be accused and put to shame again. Wherever this subject is talked about, just as the one is called blessed, so this one will hear herself called wretched and miserable and all such things. Just as the one is sung and praised not only by those who know her but also by those who do not and have received no benefit from her, so the other is reviled and slandered by those who know her and those who do not, and by those who have suffered no harm from her. Those who live rightly are praised and admired not only by their acquaintances but also by strangers, and even by their enemies. The corrupt and worthless are reviled even by their friends. This too is the work of God's providence: he has implanted in us such an affinity for virtue and such an aversion to vice that everyone votes in favor of virtue, even those who do not pursue it, and vice is condemned both by those who shun it and by those who pursue it. So it is clear that these careless women are shunned not only by those who know them but also by those who do not, and most of all by the very men who live with them. For even if they say they love and admire you greatly, even if they are grateful for this pleasure, for the very favors you grant them they hate you again [?]… [Textual notes: Savile adds “and words and looks and thought”; Savile reads “blame casts out, when”.]

and not only did you do no good, you did the greatest harm. If the women who did no good paid such a penalty, and that while their virginity remained intact, what punishment will those women undergo who, besides doing no good, did the greatest wrong to themselves, to the men living with them, and to those who were scandalized, and above all insulted the name of the Bridegroom? Do you know what a thing you have in hand, what contest you have stripped for, what part of the war you have received, what rank in the army you have been allotted? You are encamped and serving beside the very general of the war, or rather beside the king himself. In wars the whole army does not occupy one place. Some hold the wings of the battle line and others the center. Some hold the rear, others adorn the front of the phalanx, and still others appear wherever the king appears, and are seen with him everywhere and run alongside him. In the same way the choir of virgins [?] has been allotted no other rank than this. Those who wear golden robes, ride horses decked with gold, and carry shields of gold set with jewels are not meant to display the king's presence as the virgin displays the presence of Christ. They appear beside the king's royal chariot, but she, if she wishes, becomes the royal chariot herself, like the cherubim, and stands beside him like the seraphim. 7. So when she goes out into the marketplace she must appear like a statue of all philosophy and astonish everyone, like an angel just come down from heaven. If one of the cherubim themselves appeared on earth, it would turn all people toward itself. In the same way the virgin must fill everyone who sees her with wonder and astonishment at her holiness. She walks as if through a desert. She sits in church in the deepest silence. Her eye looks at none of those present, neither women nor men, but only at the Bridegroom, as if he were present and visible. When she goes home, she has again conversed with him in prayer and heard only his voice through the Scriptures, and once in the house she thinks only of her beloved. She is a stranger, a sojourner and a pilgrim, and does everything as becomes one who is a stranger to the things of this world. She flees not only the sight of men but also the company of more worldly women. She gives her body only as much attention as necessity requires and spends everything else on the care of her soul. When she is like this, who will not wonder? Who will not be amazed to see an angelic way of life in female nature? Who would dare to approach her at all? What man would choose to touch a soul on fire? So everyone will keep away, willingly or unwillingly, and everyone will be astonished, as if they were looking at gold glowing and gleaming in the fire. Gold by its very nature has great brilliance, but when it takes on the brilliance of fire as well, the marvel becomes greater and more awesome. If that is so with a material body, then when it happens to a golden soul it will be a sight longed for not only by people but by angels. Why then do you adorn yourself with clothes when you have the adornment of this flame? Clothes were not given to us so that we might make ourselves beautiful, but so that we might hide the shame of nakedness, not so that we might wear clothes that can shame us more than nakedness. That is why Adam too [was given] garments of skin… [Textual note: Savile reads “wherever”.] And if it happens that the woman who lives with him suddenly falls ill

walls are no use any more. He gets up before the others and goes in to the virgin as she lies in bed, using her illness as his excuse, since the maidservants are often slow to move. He sits beside her and takes care of other things that it is often proper for women alone to attend to. She is not ashamed and even takes pride in it. He does not blush but rejoices all the more, and the more shamefully he displays his servitude, the more he rejoices. Then that saying of the apostle, “whose glory is in their shame,” is shown in their deeds. And when the maidservants get up too, the shame is worse. Flustered and getting up in the night, they run about in his presence with their heads uncovered, in a single tunic, with bare arms. Or rather, with him moving about among them and running about with them, they are forced to do everything. What could be more shameful? And if a midwife comes as well, even then he is not ashamed, but even preens himself as strange girls come in. He has only one thing in view: to show the sick woman how he serves her. He does not know that the more he shows it, the more he shames both her and himself. And what wonder is it if he does not blush when the midwife has come? Often, even in the middle of the night, these men do not hesitate to do the work of the lowest maidservants and run for the midwife themselves. When she comes, sometimes they throw him out, however unwilling and however shameless he is, and sometimes they let him come in and sit beside the bed. Yet even if someone contrived ten thousand ways to shame him, what could he do to compare with what this man brings on himself? When day comes and both must get out of bed, there are watches and precautions. She cannot go out into the outer room without worry. Often, when she has gone out, she may have come upon the man with his body naked. And he, suspecting this very thing, sometimes announces himself before coming in and sometimes comes in without warning, and he has made himself a great laughingstock. I do not want to say more. These things, small as they are, usually kindle great coals of licentiousness. All this happens at home, and more besides. When he goes out into the marketplace and is about to come back, the indecency is greater still. Entering as if into his own house, without needing to announce himself, he has found women sitting with her and put her to shame. She too has often had the same thing happen to her. The woman has come to think it shameful to receive women, and the man men. Yet they do not refuse to live with each other, while they refuse to host each other's visitors of their own sex. What could be worse than this? Sometimes people have found him sitting beside a woman as she winds thread or holds a distaff. What could one say of the insults and the daily quarrels? Even where there is great friendship, such things are likely to happen. I have heard from some that they even suffer jealousy. Where there is no spiritual love, this is bound to happen. This is the source of the frequent falls and the corruptions, and this is how virgins become servile and shameless: even if they are not corrupted in body, they are corrupted in character. When a virgin learns to talk freely with a man, to sit with him, to look him in the face, to laugh in his presence, and to do many other unseemly things, and she thinks there is nothing terrible in it, the veil of virginity is taken away, and [?]… [Textual notes: Savile reads “allowed,” with “threw out” written above; Savile reads “going out,” Morel “I go in”.]

…her body, and after lying with him she sends him away again. But you call in the man who outrages and corrupts your soul, and you shut him up indoors all the time and do not let him leave. You bind him with heavy chains of flattery, of attentive service and of everything else you do, and you think you are winning honour when you are disgracing yourself? Tell me, then, do you not consider this present life, how short it is, how like dreams, and withering flowers, and a passing shadow? Why do you want to live in luxury now in a dream, only to be punished then in reality? And in fact the thing is not even luxury. How can it be, where there is condemnation and accusation, mockery and scandal? But even if it were luxury, what is a tiny drop of water compared with a boundless sea? “Listen, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty.” David once said this to the world when it was in a bad state. So we too sing this saying over you, changing the prophet’s words a little, and with the prophet we will say: Listen, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your wicked habit and those who live with you to your harm, and the king will desire your beauty. What could be greater for you than this? What else could we name that would equal it, when you gain as your lover the Lord of heaven and earth, of [267] angels and archangels and the powers above, and are set free from these worthless fellow servants of yours who disgrace your noble birth? So this is a good place to end my discourse, for we can say nothing equal to this [?], whether on the road or at sea.

END OF THE FIRST VOLUME.
